config.theme: Incident postmortem: the checkout outage last Tuesday
config.author: claude-opus-5-5 (Claude Code session)

cast.theme: Incident postmortem: the checkout outage last Tuesday

personas.name: Ifeoma
personas.goals: Keep it blameless and get real fixes
personas.hidden_agenda: Warned about migrations during sales in August and was ignored

personas.name: Greg
personas.goals: Make sure this never happens again
personas.hidden_agenda: The CEO yelled at him for twenty minutes

personas.name: Paolo
personas.role: Database engineer who ran the migration
personas.goals: Explain without being thrown under the bus
personas.hidden_agenda: Was told the migration was urgent by Greg's own team

personas.name: Wren
personas.goals: Get customers an apology that isn't corporate nonsense
personas.hidden_agenda: Her team worked until midnight answering emails

pack.title: Postmortem - checkout outage during the flash sale

agenda.title: What happened
agenda.goal: Establish the facts of the outage

agenda.title: Why it happened
agenda.goal: Understand why a migration ran during the sale

agenda.title: What it cost
agenda.goal: Agree the impact on customers and revenue

agenda.title: Prevention
agenda.goal: Agree the changes and their owners

facts.statement: The orders table was locked for 41 minutes
Customer service contacts about the outage = 2,450
Rolling back the migration took 22 minutes
Change freeze policy = 3 days before a sale

beats.summary: The facts; Paolo undercounts the lock and the tension starts
How the migration got through; the approval, the freeze, and an earlier warning
What it cost; the CEO number vs the real number; Wren's contact count goes unchecked
Owners, plus a fight about whether to freeze all changes

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Okay. Let's stick to facts and keep it blameless. Paolo, what happened, in order?

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: To be honest, it was a schema migration on the orders table. It started at eleven oh two.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: In the middle of the flash sale.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Greg, facts first. Paolo, what did the migration do to the table?

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: It locked it. For maybe ten minutes. Then checkout started timing out.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: From where I sit it was a lot more than ten minutes.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: How long was checkout actually down?

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: Sixty-three minutes, end to end. Including the rollback.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Sixty-three minutes. During a sale with four times normal traffic.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: And the rollback itself?

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: Twenty-two minutes. Rolling back a half-done migration is slow.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Frankly, how does this happen? Who approved a migration on sale day?

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: We'll get to why. Let's finish what.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: Honestly, from the customer side, people got charged and then got an error. That's the worst version.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Did anyone actually get charged twice?

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: A few dozen. We've refunded them already.

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: Why did our status page say everything was fine the whole time?

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Okay. Let's stick to facts. The lock was the trigger, sale traffic made it worse. Agreed?

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: Agreed.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Agreed. Now can we talk about why?

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Why. Paolo, why did it run that morning?

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: I was told it was urgent. The new returns feature needed the column.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Told by whom?

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Greg. Blameless.

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: By the returns team. Who, to be honest, report to you.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Okay. Okay. Fair.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: My team keeps texting me about the queue. Hang on.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: How many people approved the change?

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: One. The usual one.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: One person approves a change to the table that takes all our money?

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Frankly, we have a change freeze for exactly this. It's a week before any sale.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: It's three days, Greg. It's been three days since we wrote it.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Three days. Fine. Then why didn't it apply?

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: The sale was announced two days before. The freeze started after the change was already scheduled.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: So the freeze didn't know about the sale.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: To be blunt, this isn't new. We had a migration incident in August.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: August was different.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: It was the same table.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Was it? I don't remember that.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: It was. I wrote the postmortem. There was an action item to block migrations during sales. Nobody picked it up.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Then frankly, that's on leadership. That's on me.

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: To be honest, I appreciate you saying that.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: Did anyone check the lock time on the replica before running it?

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: We usually do. Not this time, because of the rush. And, okay, I said ten minutes earlier. The log says the lock was forty-one.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Forty-one minutes.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Okay. Migrations on the orders table need two approvals and a replica test, effective today.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Agreed.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Cost. Greg, what's the number the CEO has?

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Frankly, she thinks we lost a million dollars in sales. That's what she said to me.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Let's stick to facts. Finance estimates five hundred and twelve thousand.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Five twelve. That's still awful, but it's not a million. I'll correct her.

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: How many orders is that?

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: About thirty-seven hundred lost orders. Some will come back, some won't.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: From where I sit, we got about five thousand customer contacts. Email, chat, phone, all of it.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Five thousand. Wow.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: And eight hundred and sixty angry posts. Honestly, some of them were funny.

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: Funny how?

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: Someone made a meme of a shopping cart stuck in a revolving door.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: That one's actually good.

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: The one with the melting ice cream truck was better.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: The ice cream one went to the CEO's sister. She sent it to the CEO.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Of course she did.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Okay. Prevention. Let's land this.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Frankly, I want a full freeze. No changes at all during a sale.

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: To be honest, that's how we end up with a backlog of risky changes the day after.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: What about a freeze on schema changes only, from the moment a sale is announced?

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: Honestly, that makes sense to me. The sale announcement is the trigger, not a calendar.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Fine. Schema changes only.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Then schema changes are frozen from sale announcement to sale end. Decided.

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: Works for me.

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: I'll update the change policy and get it into the deploy tooling by next Friday.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: And the August action item? The one nobody picked up?

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: It's the same fix. This time it gets an owner. Me.

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: I'll write the replica lock-test script so anyone can run it before a migration.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: And the customers. We need an apology that doesn't sound like a robot wrote it.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Maybe a discount code? Ten percent?

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: Twenty. They lost an hour of their sale, honestly.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Let's think about it. I want finance's view first.

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: Someone ought to ask finance before Monday, then.

turns.speaker: Wren
turns.text: I'll draft the apology email today and send it to Greg.

turns.speaker: Paolo
turns.text: Should someone look at the returns team's other pending migrations too?

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Yes. Any pending migration on that table waits for the new process.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Who is telling the returns team their feature slips?

turns.speaker: Ifeoma
turns.text: Okay. Thank you, everyone. This was hard and you all stuck to facts. Mostly.

turns.speaker: Greg
turns.text: Mostly.
